topic: Pharmacokinetics & Pharmacodynamics of Antimicrobials — Dosing in the Septic Patient
speakerTitle: Consultant in Critical Care & Clinical Pharmacology
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Intensive Care Unit
speakerBio: An intensivist with a clinical pharmacology habit who runs the unit's therapeutic drug monitoring service and treats every dosing decision in shock as a physiology problem, not a lookup-table one.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 24-year-old with meningococcal septic shock is in your resus bay: hypotensive, third-spacing litres of fluid, kidneys hyperfiltrating on the vasopressor support. The nurse asks a simple question — "what dose of meropenem?" — and the honest answer is that the standard label dose will probably under-treat him. His volume of distribution has ballooned, his renal clearance is augmented, and the drug's killing depends on time above MIC. Getting the dose right here is not pharmacology trivia; it is the difference between a therapeutic level and a fatal under-dose. This session is about dosing the septic patient with the physiology in front of you.

1 · The two killing patterns — the master dichotomy ⚔️

Antimicrobial PK/PD splits almost every drug into one of two killing patterns, and the pattern dictates how you should dose it.

Time-dependent killingConcentration-dependent killing
Driver%T>MIC — fraction of the dosing interval the free drug stays above the MICCmax/MIC (peak height) and AUC/MIC (total exposure)
Prototype drugsβ-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems), also linezolid, macrolides (partly)Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, daptomycin, metronidazole
Dosing strategyKeep levels up — more frequent, prolonged or continuous infusionsHit high peaks — large, less frequent doses (once-daily aminoglycoside)
Post-antibiotic effectMinimal for β-lactams (levels must stay up)Prolonged (aminoglycosides keep suppressing after levels fall — allows the trough to drop)
For a β-lactam, the question is "how long are you above MIC?" For an aminoglycoside, it is "how high did you get?" Same infection, opposite dosing philosophy.

2 · β-lactams — time above MIC, and why infusions help 🕐

β-lactam killing correlates with %fT>MIC — the free (unbound) concentration exceeding the MIC for a fraction of the interval. Rough targets: ~40–50% for carbapenems, ~50–60% for penicillins, ~60–70% for cephalosporins for maximal killing; in critically ill patients many clinicians aim for 100% fT>MIC, and sometimes 4–5× MIC.

Because a standard 30-minute bolus produces a high peak that then decays below MIC before the next dose, two strategies raise %T>MIC:

  • Extended infusions — e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem given over 3–4 hours instead of 30 minutes, dramatically increasing time above MIC.
  • Continuous infusions — after a loading dose, the drug runs continuously to hold a steady concentration above MIC 24/7.
💡 Pearl

For β-lactams, frequency and infusion duration beat peak height. When an organism has a borderline-high MIC, a prolonged/continuous infusion can convert a failing regimen into a curative one — with no change in total daily dose. Loading dose first, then the infusion.

3 · Aminoglycosides & fluoroquinolones — chase the peak / the AUC 📈

  • Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin): concentration-dependent, with a long post-antibiotic effect. Target Cmax/MIC ≈ 8–10. This is why we use once-daily ("extended-interval") dosing — e.g. gentamicin ~5–7 mg/kg once daily — a big peak for efficacy, then a low trough that lets the kidney and inner ear recover, reducing nephro/ototoxicity. Monitor with a trough (and/or level on the nomogram).
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin): best predictor is AUC/MIC — target roughly >125 for Gram-negatives (lower, ~30–40, for Gram-positive pneumococcus). Cmax/MIC also matters for suppressing resistant mutants (aim ≥8–10).
⚠️ Never trough-target an aminoglycoside for efficacy

The efficacy target is the peak (Cmax/MIC 8–10); the trough is measured only to ensure it has fallen low enough to be safe (avoid accumulation and toxicity). Dosing an aminoglycoside like a time-dependent drug — small, frequent doses to 'keep a level' — maximises toxicity while blunting efficacy. Big peak, low trough.

4 · Vancomycin — AUC/MIC 400–600 and the death of trough-only dosing 🎯

Vancomycin efficacy against MRSA correlates with AUC/MIC, with a target of 400–600 (assuming MIC ≤1 mg/L). The 2020 consensus guideline (IDSA/ASHP/SIDP) moved practice away from trough-only targeting (the old 15–20 mg/L trough) toward AUC-guided dosing — using Bayesian software or two levels — because trough-only dosing over-shoots AUC and drives nephrotoxicity without added benefit.

  • Give a loading dose (e.g. 25–30 mg/kg) in serious infection to reach target fast — waiting for steady state under-treats early.
  • Maintenance ~15–20 mg/kg (actual body weight) every 8–12 h, then adjust to AUC.
  • An AUC >600 signals rising nephrotoxicity risk; <400 risks failure and resistance selection.
💡 Pearl

Vancomycin is now an AUC drug, not a trough drug. Target AUC/MIC 400–600. And always load — a septic patient cannot wait 2–3 doses to reach a therapeutic level.

5 · The septic body changes the pharmacokinetics 🌊

This is the heart of the session. Sepsis deranges every PK parameter, and it does so in directions that predispose to under-dosing the drugs that matter most.

5a · Volume of distribution ↑ — capillary leak dilutes hydrophilic drugs

Inflammatory cytokines cause capillary leak; fluid resuscitation adds litres. This expands the extracellular/interstitial space — the compartment into which hydrophilic drugs distribute. β-lactams, aminoglycosides, vancomycin and glycopeptides are hydrophilic, so their Vd rises and, for the same dose, their concentration falls. The result: standard doses produce sub-therapeutic early levels exactly when the bacterial burden is highest.

Capillary leak is a dilution problem. The sicker the patient, the bigger the tank, and the more a 'normal' dose disappears into interstitial water. This is why loading doses matter more, not less, in sepsis — and loading depends on Vd, not on renal function.

(Lipophilic drugs — fluoroquinolones, macrolides, linezolid — have large baseline Vd and are less affected by this shift.)

5b · Clearance — augmented renal clearance vs AKI

StateWhoEffect on renally-cleared drugsRisk
Augmented renal clearance (ARC)Young, previously fit, trauma/sepsis, hyperdynamic — CrCl often >130 mL/minDrug cleared faster than normalUnder-dosing & treatment failure — the commonly missed error
Acute kidney injuryShock, nephrotoxins, older/comorbidDrug cleared slower — accumulatesToxicity if not dose-reduced
⚠️ Augmented renal clearance is a silent under-doser

A young septic patient with a 'normal' or even low serum creatinine may be clearing β-lactams and vancomycin so fast that standard doses never reach target — a hidden cause of failure and resistance selection. Suspect ARC in the young, trauma, and hyperdynamic sepsis; measure a creatinine clearance rather than trusting an estimated eGFR, and dose up (larger/more frequent doses, prolonged infusions, therapeutic drug monitoring).

5c · Renal replacement therapy (CRRT)

CRRT provides its own, substantial clearance of hydrophilic, low-protein-bound drugs. The classic and dangerous error is to renally dose-reduce a patient on CRRT as if anuric — CRRT clears these drugs efficiently, so β-lactams and vancomycin often need doses closer to normal (or higher) than the 'anuric' reduction would suggest. Under-dosing on CRRT is a well-recognised cause of treatment failure; use CRRT-specific dosing and TDM.

5d · Hypoalbuminaemia

For highly protein-bound drugs (e.g. ceftriaxone, ertapenem, teicoplanin, flucloxacillin), the low albumin of critical illness raises the free fraction — increasing both clearance and the active concentration, complicating prediction and often shortening effective exposure.

6 · Loading doses — the one number sepsis cannot wait for 💉

A loading dose is determined by volume of distribution, not clearance — so it is independent of renal function. Whether the patient is anuric or hyperfiltrating, they still need the full loading dose to reach a therapeutic concentration quickly. Skipping or reducing the load 'because the kidneys are bad' is a fundamental error: you delay reaching target at the very moment the bacterial burden and mortality risk are highest.

  • Vancomycin: load 25–30 mg/kg regardless of renal function.
  • Aminoglycoside: full weight-based dose for the first dose; adjust interval, not the loading amount, for renal impairment.
  • β-lactams: a loading dose (or first dose as a bolus) before starting a continuous/extended infusion.

7 · Putting it together — a mental algorithm 🧠

  1. Classify the drug: time-dependent (β-lactam) or concentration-dependent (aminoglycoside/fluoroquinolone) — and hydrophilic or lipophilic.
  2. Load based on Vd (expanded in sepsis) — independent of kidneys.
  3. Choose the pattern: β-lactam → prolonged/continuous infusion for %T>MIC; aminoglycoside → once-daily big peak; vancomycin → AUC/MIC 400–600.
  4. Assess clearance: ARC (dose up) vs AKI (dose down) vs CRRT (don't under-dose).
  5. Monitor: TDM for vancomycin (AUC), aminoglycosides (peak for efficacy, trough for safety), and increasingly β-lactams where available.
☠️ M&M — the young man who was 'renally dosed' to death's door

A 28-year-old with Pseudomonas bacteraemia and septic shock was started on meropenem 500 mg every 12 hours — a reduced dose, chosen because his creatinine had bumped on admission and someone 'renally adjusted' it. In fact he had augmented renal clearance: within 24 hours his creatinine normalised and his true CrCl was >160 mL/min. On the low, infrequent, bolus-dosed meropenem his %T>MIC never came close to target against a borderline-MIC Pseudomonas. He remained bacteraemic and febrile for four days; a resistant subpopulation was selected, pushing the MIC higher. Only when the ID team recognised ARC, gave a loading dose and switched to 2 g every 8 hours as a 3-hour extended infusion did he clear the infection. Lesson: in the young hyperdynamic septic patient, the danger is under-dosing, not over-dosing. Load by Vd, dose by real clearance, and use the killing pattern — reflexive 'renal adjustment' on a single high creatinine nearly cost him his life and bred resistance in the process.

8 · Take-home 🎓

  • Two killing patterns: β-lactams = time-dependent (%T>MIC → extended/continuous infusions); aminoglycosides & fluoroquinolones = concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC 8–10; AUC/MIC).
  • Vancomycin is an AUC drug: target AUC/MIC 400–600, not a trough — and always load 25–30 mg/kg.
  • Sepsis expands Vd via capillary leak → hydrophilic drugs (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, vancomycin) are diluted and under-dosed. Loading doses matter more, not less.
  • Augmented renal clearance silently under-doses the young septic patient — suspect it, measure CrCl, dose up.
  • Don't under-dose on CRRT — it clears these drugs efficiently; anuric dosing causes failure.
  • Loading dose depends on Vd, not clearance — give the full load whatever the kidneys are doing.

moderatorQs.q: Explain to the panel why a β-lactam and an aminoglycoside should be dosed in opposite ways.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because their killing is driven by different PK/PD indices. β-lactams are time-dependent: efficacy tracks %fT>MIC, the fraction of the interval free drug stays above the MIC, and they have little post-antibiotic effect — so you keep levels up with frequent, prolonged or continuous infusions. Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent with a long post-antibiotic effect: efficacy tracks Cmax/MIC (target ~8–10), so you give a large once-daily dose for a high peak, then let the trough fall low to allow renal and cochlear recovery and reduce toxicity. Same infection, opposite philosophy: for the β-lactam ask 'how long above MIC?', for the aminoglycoside ask 'how high did the peak get?'

moderatorQs.q: How has vancomycin dosing changed, and what target do you now use?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Vancomycin killing against MRSA correlates with AUC/MIC, and the 2020 IDSA/ASHP/SIDP consensus moved practice from trough-only targeting (the old 15–20 mg/L) to AUC-guided dosing with a target AUC/MIC of 400–600 (MIC ≤1). The reason is safety as much as efficacy: trough-only dosing tends to overshoot the AUC and drive nephrotoxicity without extra benefit, while an AUC <400 risks failure and resistance. Practically that means a loading dose of 25–30 mg/kg to hit target fast, maintenance ~15–20 mg/kg every 8–12 h, and Bayesian or two-level AUC monitoring rather than chasing a trough number.

moderatorQs.q: A young trauma patient with sepsis has a normal creatinine but keeps spiking fevers on standard-dose piperacillin–tazobactam. What is your leading concern?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Augmented renal clearance causing systematic under-dosing. Young, previously fit, hyperdynamic trauma/sepsis patients frequently have a CrCl >130 mL/min despite a 'normal' or even low serum creatinine, clearing hydrophilic β-lactams faster than standard dosing can replace — so %T>MIC never reaches target and the infection smoulders, selecting resistance. On top of that, capillary leak has expanded the volume of distribution, diluting the drug further. I would measure a creatinine clearance rather than trust eGFR, give a loading dose, and dose up — larger and/or more frequent doses given as a prolonged/continuous infusion to maximise time above MIC, with TDM where available. The instinct to 'renally reduce' here would be exactly backwards.

audienceQs.q: My patient is on CRRT — do I use the anuric renal dose for their antibiotics?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — that is a classic and dangerous error. CRRT provides substantial clearance of hydrophilic, low-protein-bound drugs like β-lactams and vancomycin, so dosing them as if the patient were anuric leads to sub-therapeutic levels and treatment failure. Use CRRT-specific dosing (which is generally closer to normal renal dosing, sometimes higher, and depends on the effluent/filtration rate), give the full loading dose regardless, and use therapeutic drug monitoring for vancomycin and, where available, β-lactams. The default assumption on CRRT should be 'don't under-dose,' not 'reduce because the native kidneys aren't working.'

audienceQs.q: Why do you insist on a loading dose even when renal function is poor?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because a loading dose is determined by the volume of distribution, not by clearance — so it is independent of renal function. The load's job is to fill the (sepsis-expanded) distribution volume and reach a therapeutic concentration quickly, at the moment bacterial burden and mortality risk are highest; clearance only governs the maintenance dose that follows. Reducing or skipping the load 'because the kidneys are bad' delays reaching target by two or three half-lives and under-treats early. So for vancomycin I load 25–30 mg/kg whatever the eGFR, give a full first aminoglycoside dose and lengthen only the interval for poor renal function, and bolus-load β-lactams before an infusion.

audienceQs.q: Which antibiotics are most affected by the capillary leak and fluid resuscitation of sepsis?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The hydrophilic ones — β-lactams, aminoglycosides, and vancomycin/glycopeptides. Capillary leak plus litres of resuscitation fluid expand the extracellular/interstitial space these drugs distribute into, so their volume of distribution rises and the concentration from a standard dose falls, producing sub-therapeutic early levels exactly when you need them most. Lipophilic agents — fluoroquinolones, macrolides, linezolid — already have a large baseline Vd and are relatively spared. The practical consequence: for the hydrophilic drugs in a leaking, resuscitated septic patient, loading doses matter more, not less, and you should expect to need higher or more frequent dosing than the label suggests.
